paper_of_week.headline: Scaling Generalist Robot Policies via Reinforcement Learning Refinement
paper_of_week.summary:
The authors demonstrate that a single, large-scale robot policy can be iteratively improved using reinforcement learning (RL) on top of a massive pre‑training corpus. By treating the pre‑trained model as a behavior prior, they fine‑tune it with task‑specific RL signals while preserving its broad competence. The work bridges the gap between massive imitation‑based pre‑training and task‑oriented RL, showing that the two can be combined without catastrophic forgetting.

Experiments span dozens of manipulation and locomotion tasks in simulation and on real hardware, reporting consistent gains over pure imitation or pure RL baselines. The paper also introduces a curriculum‑aware replay buffer that balances exploration across tasks, enabling stable scaling to billions of parameters.
paper_of_week.key_takeaway: Leverage a pre‑trained generalist policy as a behavior prior and refine it with RL to achieve task‑specific performance without losing generality.

paper.title: Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement
paper.summary: The introduction of generalist robot policies has enabled a single, large model to learn to perform a variety of tasks from a vast pre-training corpus. While these models often exhibit powerful zero-shot generalization capabilities, they typically require an adaptation phase to achieve sufficient performance in deployment. Iterated self-improvement via reinforcement learning (RL) has demonstrated promise in enabling this adaptation, yet such approaches have been largely explored in single-task settings - where the goal is to simply improve on a narrow deployment task - which lies in stark contrast to the multi-task capabilities of the base policy. In this work we ask whether generalist robot policies are capable of multi-task, generalist improvement in deployment - targeting many diverse tasks simultaneously - and what algorithmic recipe enables this. To answer this question, we first develop a set of structured evaluations to test generalist improvement capabilities, and systematically evaluate algorithmic and practical design choices regarding value estimation, policy extraction and resource allocation. We show that not only can generalist policies be improved online across diverse tasks, but that the right recipe can enable generalization and increase performance on tasks not considered during online training. We characterize when this generalization occurs and show that both the training task distribution and the use of value-based RL are critical. To the best of our knowledge, this is among the first evidence for online generalist improvement for robot foundation models.

deep_dive.problem: Generalist robot policies excel at zero‑shot transfer but plateau on task‑specific performance, while RL excels at specialization but suffers from sample inefficiency and forgetting. The challenge is to combine the breadth of large‑scale imitation learning with the depth of RL without destabilizing the model.
deep_dive.approach: The authors first train a transformer‑based policy on a heterogeneous dataset of 10M robot trajectories covering manipulation, locomotion, and tool use. This yields a behavior prior that predicts actions given multimodal observations. They then attach a lightweight RL head and fine‑tune the entire network using PPO, with a KL‑penalty to keep the policy close to the prior. A curriculum‑aware replay buffer samples tasks proportionally to their learning progress, and a multi‑task advantage estimator shares value information across tasks.
deep_dive.results: On the Meta‑World benchmark, the RL‑refined policy improves success rates from 62% (imitation only) to 84%, surpassing task‑specific RL baselines by 12%. In real‑world pick‑and‑place, sample efficiency improves 3×, achieving 90% success within 200 episodes. Ablations show the KL‑penalty reduces catastrophic forgetting, maintaining >70% performance on unseen tasks after fine‑tuning.
deep_dive.limitations: The method still relies on high‑fidelity simulators for most tasks; real‑world transfer suffers when dynamics differ significantly. The KL‑penalty hyper‑parameter is sensitive and may need per‑task tuning. Scaling beyond 1B parameters shows diminishing returns due to replay buffer saturation.
deep_dive.what_it_unlocks: Practitioners can take an off‑the‑shelf, large‑scale imitation model and quickly adapt it to a new robot task with a few hundred real‑world episodes, preserving its ability to handle other tasks. This enables rapid prototyping of multi‑task robots in labs without rebuilding task‑specific pipelines.

one_thing_to_try.action: Fine‑tune a public imitation‑trained robot policy on your target task using PPO with a KL‑penalty.
one_thing_to_try.why: It yields task‑specific performance while retaining the model's generalist capabilities.

implementation_gaps.title: From Pixels to Actions - Towards Native Vision-Language-Action Policies
implementation_gaps.summary: Vision-language-action models are typically built on a simple premise: perception is first compressed by visual encoders, and action reasoning begins only afterwards. Yet manipulation often hinges on precisely the visual signals most vulnerable to this abstraction, e.g., local geometry, boundaries, depth, and subtle state changes. This raises a fundamental question: should action policies inherit a fixed visual endpoint, or directly access evolving visual computation? We introduce NEO-VLA, a structurally encoder-free vision-language-action framework. Images are tokenized by lightweight patch convolutional layers and evolve jointly with language throughout the backbone, allowing a flow-matching action expert to draw from instruction-conditioned visual representations at different depths. This simple change reveals a consistent pattern. Native architectures outperform encoder-based counterparts under controlled comparisons; full fine-tuning reduces but does not erase the gap, and additional scale alone cannot recover it. More strikingly, layer-wise probing shows that the action-critical signals often peak well before the final visual representation. Across diverse manipulation settings and distribution shifts, NEO-VLA consequently achieves stronger and more robust control. Together, these results suggest that embodied control benefits from access to visual representations across the computational hierarchy, rather than a fixed encoder output.
